questions.prompt: Which approach best supports reliable work with Calling Native Functionality?
options: Skip input validation because Node.js applications run on a trusted server.
Assume every supported runtime has identical APIs and scheduling behavior.
Store credentials and production secrets directly in the source file.
Treat TypeScript integration as optional and version-sensitive; separate type-checking/build steps from runtime assumptions.
questions.answer_key: Treat TypeScript integration as optional and version-sensitive; separate type-checking/build steps from runtime assumptions.
questions.explanation: Treat TypeScript integration as optional and version-sensitive; separate type-checking/build steps from runtime assumptions. The example and verification steps should make this practice observable.

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under Calling Native Functionality?
questions.explanation: “Native add-on concepts” is one of the subtopics retained from the supplied Node.js curriculum for this lesson.

questions.prompt: Before relying on a Calling Native Functionality implementation, what verification is most useful?
options: Use the same code regardless of documented version differences.
Verify the documented result in a supported runtime and test one failure or boundary case.
Assume the API behaves as expected without running a check.
Ignore failures so the program continues silently.
questions.answer_key: Verify the documented result in a supported runtime and test one failure or boundary case.
questions.explanation: A small deterministic check plus a failure/boundary case helps distinguish a correct design from a happy-path-only example.
